articles.title: ‘The Riverbank,’ ‘Elza’ Top Rio Film Festival Awards as ‘On Behalf of My Son,’ ‘The French Teacher’ and ‘London’ Scoop Key Prizes
articles.summary: Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias’ Locarno-winning “The Riverbank” has taken Best Fiction Feature Film at this year’s Rio Film Festival, with Eryk Rocha’s “Elza” scoring Best Documentary Feature Film.
body: Other major Brazilian films of the year have also taken top awards, including Gabriel Martins’s Toronto-selected “On Behalf of My Son,” Venice-selected “London” by Victor di Marco and Márcio Picoli, and Ricardo Alves Jr.’s “The French Teacher,” which just bowed at San Sebastián.

This year’s Premiére Brasil jury was presided over by veteran “La Bola Negra” producer Esther García and also included co-director of programming at the Berlinale, Jacqueline Lyanga; French producer Sophie Erbs; composer Flavia Tygel; and casting director Marcela Altberg.

The New Trends jury was presided over by director and editor Karen Harley; screenwriter Maira Oliveira; producer Dora Amorim; director and screenwriter Guto Parente. The Felix Jury, dedicated to films broaching LGBTQIA+ issues, was presided over by lawyer Ericka Gavinho; director and screenwriter Clara Anastacia; cultural critic Guilherme Terri, also known as Rita Von Hunty; filmmaker Vita; and cultural programmer Rodrigo Gerace.

articles.title: ‘Bedford Park’ Star and Busan Juror Moon Choi on Locking Away Her Trophies and Plotting a Screen Version of a Molière-Winning Play
articles.summary: For several years after the biggest run of her career, Moon Choi, known in Korea as Choi Hee-seo, kept her trophies out of sight. The haul was substantial. Her turn as Japanese anarchist Kaneko Fumiko in “Anarchist from Colony” swept Korea’s new actress prizes, and her lead role in independent…
body: “I felt that being successful at a young age can do some bad things to you. It didn’t make me feel proud, but it actually kind of made me feel crestfallen because I felt like I had to reach a height that goes beyond those awards,” she says.

What followed was a stretch she describes candidly: more independent films, Korean TV series that “flopped really badly” and film “A Girl with Closed Eyes” with Kim Minha that still has no release date two years after its Busan premiere. Through all of it, she was waiting for “ Bedford Park.”

Choi is now back in Busan in a different role, sitting on the seven-member jury for the festival’s competition section, which is only in its second year. Zhang Yimou presides over a panel that also includes Bi Gan, Kei Ishikawa, July Jung, Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Kazakh actor Samal Yeslyamova. “Bedford Park” is also in town, screening in the Flash Forward section.

“I don’t have the pressure that I need to prove anything to anybody,” Choi says of returning as a juror. “I’m kind of feeling like a student trying to learn from all these films that I’m going to be watching alongside amazing people like Zhang Yimou and Bi Gan.”

articles.title: How Busan Title ‘Selvi’ Turns a Nurse’s Working Hours Into an Endurance Test
articles.summary: A homecare nurse whose working day stretches from 12 hours to 72 sits at the center of “Selvi,” the first feature from Tamil filmmaker Sailesh Rathnakumar, which premieres in the Busan International Film Festival’s Vision–Asia section.
body: “For someone like Selvi, a crisis doesn’t necessarily arrive as one dramatic event,” Rathnakumar tells Variety. “It develops through a series of working hours, additional responsibilities and small compromises that gradually become unbearable.”
The jump from 12 to 24, 48 and then 72 hours gave the story its shape, he says. As the clock runs, Selvi is always on hand for someone else and has less and less time to be a person in her own right.

The film opens on a beach, with Selvi and her friends flying kites, before moving into domestic interiors where her world narrows. “With the kites, I wanted to show the possibility of looking upwards, of imagining something beyond the immediate circumstances of one’s life,” Rathnakumar says.

The production took its time finding homes that felt lived in and signaled the class of the families inside them. “Selvi can be essential to a family’s everyday life without ever being treated as someone who belongs to it,” he says.

articles.title: Box Office Boom for China’s Women Directors Feeds New Parallax Films Pickups From Shao Yihui, Yin Lichuan and Yang Lina (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Three filmmakers at the forefront of China’s women-led cinema boom – Shao Yihui, Yang Lina and Yin Lichuan – have new titles on the slate of sales agent Parallax Films, which is shopping them to buyers at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan.
body: Veteran director Yin’s “A Joke” is billed as the first Chinese feature to tackle sexual harassment in the workplace. It follows a sanitation worker who spends three years quietly collecting proof against her abusive boss, then joins forces with a young lawyer to expose him.

The pickups ride a wave that began in 2021 with Shao’s breakout “B for Busy,” which opened the door for female-centered stories in China. Three years later, Yin’s “Like a Rolling Stone” and Shao’s second feature “Her Story” grossed more than RMB845 million ($118 million) combined at the domestic box office.

“Her Story” went on to win best picture, best actress and best supporting actress at the 38th Golden Rooster Awards, mainland China’s government-backed film honors. Films by women directors have historically won few opportunities at the awards, making the haul a landmark for feminist filmmaking in the country.

articles.title: Kelly Clarkson Responds After New York Store Denies She Got the ‘Pretty Woman’ Treatment: “You’re a Liar”
articles.summary: "It’s not that hard to be kind," she wrote after Art of Play shot down her version of events. "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t."
body: Kelly Clarkson has responded to a New York shop’s denial that she got the Pretty Woman treatment while shopping in their store.

According to its website, Brooklyn-based Art of Play sells home goods, puzzles, games, toys and books and also features a 26-seat theater that hosts performances by magicians. On Sunday, Art of Play responded on its social media, denying Clarkson’s version of events.

“Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying ‘Molly,’ a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here,” the post reads. “Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale. However, the negative experience Kelly described on twitter would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop.

“At Art of Play whether someone comes in to make a purchase or simply look around for a while, they are equally welcome. We greet everyone who walks in the door with the invitation to ‘pick things up and play.’ And they do, many stay for hours enjoying our puzzles, games and toys.
points: "It’s not that hard to be kind," she wrote after Art of Play shot down her version of events.
"I never blast people but you my friend were an exception.

articles.title: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey
articles.summary: The makers of Coraline return with their distinctive animation style in a magical tale of a secret world of strange beasts, talking animals and evil governesses. Here is an engaging family movie from the Portland-based Laika studio that created Coraline.
body: They are stunned when a bunch (or rather a murder) of crows gather with Hitchcockian menace in a kids’ play area, swoop down and carry poor little Mac off to their forest domain. Plucky (and also terrified) Prue and Curtis give chase and enter the dark and trackless forest, and find it is a parallel world, undreamt of by the ordinary human world, populated by all manner of loquacious beasts and oppressed humans. Their rule is divided between the supercilious and incompetent governor (Marc Evan Jackson) and the evil dowager governess, voiced with relish by Carey Mulligan, who has at her command a redcoat army of coyotes.

The dowager governess has a wrenching sadness in her heart, due to an awful loss and a tragic attempt at a cover-up, which the film shows us in the opening section. Prue and Curtis, though separated by the action, are to come together for their big showdown with this wicked witch of the forest and a reckoning also with the Wildwood’s bandit leader and freedom fighter Brendan, voiced by Mahershala Ali.

articles.title: Another Marvel Director Nearly Made The Young Sheldon Pilot
articles.summary: The Young Sheldon pilot was helmed by Iron Man director Jon Favreau, but if he hadn't been available another Marvel director was next on the list.
body: Jon Favreau is about as accomplished as one can be in the realm of directing successful projects. No only did he help kickstart the Marvel Cinematic Universe with "Iron Man," but he's also behind several hugely successful TV shows as well. The first one that comes to mind is "The Mandalorian" in the "Star Wars" galaxy, but he also directed the pilot for "The Big Bang Theory" spin-off "Young Sheldon." If he hadn't, though, another Marvel director very well could have.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, series co-creator Steve Molaro explained that Favreau was the first choice, as Chuck Lorre was a fan. "I had a friendship with Jon Favreau, so when we were floating around who would be a great fit, I told Chuck I kind of know him," Molaro said. He further explained that it was 2016's "The Jungle Book" that really got things going.
At the time, Favreau was also working on 2019's "The Lion King" remake, but he still managed to carve out some time to direct the "Young Sheldon" pilot.

articles.title: Paramount Is Both The Best And Worst Thing To Happen To Avatar: The Last Airbender
articles.summary: Paramount has repeatedly fumbled the Avatar: The Last Airbender franchise, but announcements at New York Comic-Con 2026 offer hope of a turnaround.
body: With its spectacular combination of epic fantasy, nuanced storytelling, compelling characters, mature themes, and stunning martial arts action, "Avatar: The Last Airbender" is one of the greatest shows of the 21st century.

It's been over 20 years since "The Last Airbender" premiered, and since then we've had dozens of books and comics, two live-action remakes, two sequel series, and one sequel movie. In theory, a great time to be an "Avatar" fan, right? In 2026 alone we've had the very first feature film animation in the franchise, with the return of Aang and his friends as young adults in a brand new adventure. And most recently we got "Avatar: Seven Havens," the first new series in over a decade, with the next avatar in the cycle – actually, two Avatars.
points: Paramount has repeatedly fumbled the Avatar: The Last Airbender franchise, but announcements at New York Comic-Con 2026 offer hope of a turnaround.

articles.title: Non-Alcoholic Drink Pairings Up Their Game (and their Prices) at L.A.’s Top Restaurants
articles.summary: Alcohol consumption has plummeted so drastically in L.A. that establishments are offering elevated zero-proof accompaniments to make their margins.
body: Kim Stodel, bar director at three-Michelin-starred Providence a few blocks west of the Paramount lot in Hollywood, steeps charred sweet corn in jasmine green tea on a recent afternoon. “I have a suspicion that adding this burnt aroma will accentuate things, taking it over the edge in the way I’m hoping,” he explains of tweaking this accompaniment to an abalone dish on the seafood restaurant’s tasting menu. It’s part of Stodel’s extensive prep and constant experimentation for his nonalcoholic pairings program.

Providence has been around for two decades, Stodel overseeing drinks for more than half that span. But he’s only been concocting elaborate spirit-free progressions in the past two years. “The NA category is exploding,” Stodel says, “and we’re all still beginners, exploring.” Related Stories. articles.title: William Shatner's '70s Sci-Fi TV Movie Featured A Guest-Star From A Notorious Star Trek Episode
articles.summary: William Shatner and Kim Darby both appeared in the 1972 TV movie The People, but they also acted together in a controversial Star Trek episode.
body: In 1972, Francis Ford Coppola served as the executive producer for John Korty's TV movie "The People," based largely on the story "Pottage" by celebrated sci-fi author Zenna Henderson. "The People" stars Kim Darby as a schoolteacher named Malodye, who travels out to a very, very remote community to teach the local children. The community is very Amish-like in their customs and very eerie. The children, for instance, are forbidden from doing any of the fun things that Melodye suggests during class. Indeed, the very concept of "fun" seems to be banned.

The sci-fi twist is that all the members of this community are actually extraterrestrials who emigrated to Earth when they lost their home planet to environmental disasters. The aliens have been on Earth since the late 19th century, but have long been attacked and pilloried for their mild alien superpowers. The overall film is super-mellow, with William Shatner playing a character named Dr. Curtis. Coppola's father, Carmine, wrote the score. The movie is pastoral and calm and doesn't really seem to feature much in the way of actual drama.
points: William Shatner and Kim Darby both appeared in the 1972 TV movie The People, but they also acted together in a controversial Star Trek episode.

articles.title: Marshals Season 2 May Finally Give An Overlooked Yellowstone Character A Real Storyline
articles.summary: Yellowstone character Tate Dutton hasn't been give much to do, but he might finally be getting an real storyline in Marshals Season 2.
body: "Marshals" has been flirting with giving Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton a storyline for a while. Every now and then the show seems to be forging ahead with an arc for this "Yellowstone" alum only to pull back and leave us wondering why he's in the series at all. Season 2, Episode 2, "End of Watch," once again suggests "Marshals" is actually interested in Kayce Dutton's son, but whether this will go anywhere remains to be seen.

"Marshals" Season 1 struggled to figure out what it was actually about, balancing so many characters and storylines that it ultimately ended up being a very confused and confusing experience. In many ways, the writers are hamstrung by the network procedural format, which requires they introduce and solve a new case every week. But when you have an expansive new ensemble to get to know and a lead character with considerable "Yellowstone" baggage to unpack, effectively executing the whole case-of-the-week thing becomes very difficult.
